They next passed some deserted brickworks. The fog was thinner here, allowing him to see the odd, bottle-shaped kilns and the orange flames spreading from them like fans. A dog barked as they passed, and somewhere far off in the darkness a stray seagull cried. The horse caught its foot in a rut, swerved, and began to gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and rattled once more along roughly paved streets. Most windows were dark, but here and there strange shadows stood out against a blind lit from behind. He watched them with curiosity. They moved like monstrous puppets, making gestures as though they were alive. He hated them. A heavy anger filled his heart. As they rounded a corner, a woman shouted something from an open doorway, and two men chased the cab for about a hundred yards. The driver struck at them with his whip.

People say that strong feelings make our thoughts go round in circles. Certainly Dorian Gray's bitten lips kept forming the same clever words about the soul and the senses, repeating them with horrible persistence. At last they seemed to express his mood completely. By agreeing with their argument, he justified desires that would have ruled him even without an excuse. The single thought spread through every part of his brain. The fierce desire to live, the most terrible of all human cravings, brought each trembling nerve and muscle to life. Ugliness had once disgusted him because it made things real. Now he welcomed it for exactly that reason. Ugliness was the only reality. The rough street fight, the disgusting hideout, the raw violence of chaotic lives, even the wickedness of thieves and outcasts, felt more intensely real than all the beautiful forms of art or the dreamy images of songs. He needed these things to help him forget. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the driver pulled up sharply at the entrance to a dark lane. Black ships' masts rose above the low rooftops and uneven chimney stacks. Strands of white mist hung from their crossbars like ghostly sails.

“Somewhere round here, sir, isn't it?” he asked hoarsely through the hatch.

Dorian gave a start and looked around. “This will do,” he replied. He hurried out, paid the driver the extra fare he had promised, and walked quickly toward the quay. Here and there a lantern shone at the stern of an enormous merchant ship. Its light trembled and broke into fragments in the puddles. A steamer being loaded with coal before departure cast a red glow. The slimy pavement looked like a wet raincoat.

Yet he had oppressed no one and imprisoned no one. Far from ruthlessly collecting what was owed to him, he had voluntarily surrendered his claims, ventured into a world that offered him no special favors, established an independent place in it, and earned his own living. Monsieur Gabelle had managed the impoverished, debt-burdened estate under written orders to spare the people and give them whatever little could be given: as much winter fuel as the demanding creditors would allow, and as much summer produce as could be rescued from their grasp. Surely, in defending himself, Gabelle had cited these instructions and produced them as evidence. They were bound to come to light now.

This supported the desperate decision Charles Darnay was beginning to reach: he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the sailor in the old tale, winds and currents had carried him within reach of the Magnetic Rock. It was pulling him toward it, and he had to go. Every thought that entered his mind swept him onward, faster and faster, ever more steadily toward that terrible attraction. Beneath the surface, he had been troubled by the knowledge that wicked purposes were being pursued by wicked agents in his own unhappy country. He could not help knowing himself to be better than those men, yet he was absent instead of trying to prevent bloodshed and uphold the claims of mercy and humanity. This uneasiness, partly suppressed and partly accusing him, had prepared him for the sharp comparison between himself and the courageous old gentleman with his powerful sense of duty. That comparison, which reflected badly on him, had immediately been followed by Monseigneur's sneers, which wounded him deeply, and Stryver's, which for old reasons were especially coarse and infuriating. Then came Gabelle's letter: an innocent prisoner facing death, appealing to his justice, his honor, and his good name.

He had made his decision. He must go to Paris.

Yes. The Magnetic Rock was drawing him in, and he must sail onward until he struck it. He knew nothing of any rock; he could scarcely see a danger. The intentions behind his actions, unfinished though those actions were, made them appear to him in a light that France would gratefully recognize once he arrived to explain them. Then the glorious prospect of doing good rose before him, that hopeful mirage which so often appears to well-intentioned minds. Carried away by the illusion, he even imagined himself exercising some influence over the raging Revolution, helping to guide it as it ran so terrifyingly out of control.

Once this was done, I released a few more loops from the rim, pushed another section of cloth through, and attached those loops to their matching buttons. Working this way, I could fit the bag's entire upper section between the netting and the hoop. The hoop would now clearly fall inside the basket, leaving the buttons alone to support the full weight of the basket and everything in it. At first this might seem unsafe, but it was not. The buttons themselves were very strong, and they sat so close together that each carried only a tiny share of the total weight. In fact, I would not have worried even if the basket and its contents had weighed three times as much. I then lifted the hoop back up inside the rubber covering. Using three lightweight poles made for the purpose, I supported it almost as high as before. This kept the top of the bag spread open and held the lower part of the netting in its proper place. All I still needed to do was seal the opening at the top. That was easily managed: I gathered the folds of material together and twisted them tightly from inside with a fixed device resembling a tourniquet.

“Three round panes of thick, clear glass had been fitted into the sides of the covering that now enclosed the basket. Through them I could easily look around me in every horizontal direction. A fourth window of the same kind was set into the cloth underneath, aligned with a small hole in the basket's floor. This allowed me to look straight down. I had found it impossible, however, to fit a similar window above me. The unusual way the opening was sealed left wrinkles in the cloth that prevented it. I therefore could not expect to see anything directly overhead. This hardly mattered, of course, since even if I had managed to install a window at the top, the balloon itself would have blocked the view and made it useless.

“About a foot below one of the side windows was a round opening eight inches across. It had a brass rim with a screw thread cut into its inner edge. The condenser's large tube screwed into this rim, while the body of the machine remained, of course, inside the rubber chamber.
